input: Cancer treatment can diminish quality of life (QOL), and age may influence supportive-care benefits. This randomized trial examined whether older adults (age 65 years or older) and younger adults (age 18-64 years) with newly diagnosed advanced cancer differed in response to a comprehensive QOL intervention during radiation therapy. Patients in the parent trial were randomly assigned to the intervention or control group; this age-group analysis focused on intervention recipients. The intervention comprised six 90-minute multidisciplinary sessions addressing physical, emotional, social, spiritual, and functional QOL. QOL and mood were assessed at baseline and weeks 4, 27, and 52 with the Linear Analogue Self-Assessment (LASA), Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-General (FACT-G), and Profile of Mood States (POMS). Among 131 randomized patients, 54 intervention participants were evaluable, including 16 older adults and 38 younger adults. Across follow-up, older adults reported higher overall QOL (LASA 74.4 vs. 62.9, p = 0.040), greater social well-being (FACT-G 91.1 vs. 83.3, p = 0.045), and less anger-hostility (POMS 95.0 vs. 86.4, p = 0.028) than younger adults. By week 4, mean improvement from baseline in LASA overall QOL was 8.1 points in older adults and 2.6 points in younger adults (between-group p = 0.048), indicating an early separation in perceived QOL. The age difference in anger-hostility persisted at week 27 (92.2 vs. 84.2, p = 0.027) and week 52 (96.3 vs. 85.9, p = 0.005). In contrast, physical and functional well-being did not differ significantly by age at week 52 (physical: 23.8 vs. 22.9, p = 0.41; functional: 21.7 vs. 21.1, p = 0.56). Completion of at least five sessions was similar in older and younger adults (81% vs. 79%), and no serious adverse event was attributed to the intervention. Comparable completion and absence of serious intervention-related harms suggested that the program was feasible in both age groups. Taken together, the age-associated advantage was concentrated in overall QOL and selected psychosocial domains rather than being uniform across all QOL dimensions. Because the comparison included only 16 older intervention participants and was not the primary randomization contrast, these subgroup findings should be considered exploratory rather than definitive evidence of an age-by-treatment interaction. Older adults receiving the multidisciplinary QOL intervention during advanced cancer treatment appeared to derive greater benefit in selected QOL domains than younger adults, with especially durable differences in anger-hostility; further study should determine whether supportive-care strategies should be tailored by age.

A platinum compound combined with a taxane is standard first-line chemotherapy for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, but paclitaxel-related neurotoxicity can limit treatment tolerability. This randomized trial compared docetaxel-carboplatin with paclitaxel-carboplatin as initial chemotherapy for patients with stage Ic-IV epithelial ovarian or primary peritoneal cancer. A total of 1077 patients were randomly assigned to docetaxel 75 mg/m2 by 1-hour intravenous infusion or paclitaxel 175 mg/m2 by 3-hour infusion, each followed by carboplatin targeted to an area under the concentration-time curve of 5 every 3 weeks for six cycles; responding patients could receive up to three additional cycles of carboplatin alone. Progression-free survival was the principal efficacy outcome, with overall survival, tumor and CA-125 responses, treatment delivery, toxicity, and quality of life also assessed. After a median follow-up of 23 months, progression-free survival was similar between groups: median progression-free survival was 15.0 months with docetaxel-carboplatin and 14.8 months with paclitaxel-carboplatin (hazard ratio [HR] 0.97, 95% CI 0.83-1.13; P=.707), while 2-year overall survival was 64.2% and 68.9%, respectively (HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.92-1.39; P=.238). Objective tumor response rates were 58.7% with docetaxel-carboplatin and 59.5% with paclitaxel-carboplatin (difference -0.8%, 95% CI -8.6% to 7.1%; P=.868), and CA-125 response rates were 75.8% and 76.8%, respectively (difference -1.0%, 95% CI -7.2% to 5.1%; P=.794). The absence of meaningful differences in progression-free survival and response indicates that docetaxel-carboplatin achieved antitumor activity comparable to paclitaxel-carboplatin during the available follow-up. Grade 2 or higher neurosensory toxicity was substantially less frequent with docetaxel-carboplatin than with paclitaxel-carboplatin (11% vs 30%; absolute difference 19%, 95% CI 15%-24%; P<.001), and grade 2 or higher neuromotor toxicity was also reduced (3% vs 7%; absolute difference 4%, 95% CI 1%-7%; P<.001). In contrast, grade 3-4 neutropenia occurred more often with docetaxel-carboplatin (94% vs 84%; absolute difference 11%, 95% CI 7%-14%; P<.001), and febrile or otherwise clinically significant neutropenic complications were more frequent (10.4% vs 5.6%; P=.006). Despite greater myelosuppression, 78% of docetaxel-treated patients and 76% of paclitaxel-treated patients completed all six planned combination cycles, median delivered dose intensity exceeded 94% in both groups, and treatment-related discontinuation was uncommon (6.1% vs 5.8%; P=.84). Serious nonhematologic adverse events and treatment-related mortality were not increased with docetaxel-carboplatin. The toxicity profile therefore differed rather than uniformly favoring one regimen: docetaxel-carboplatin substantially reduced clinically important neurotoxicity but produced more hematologic suppression. Preserved cycle completion and dose intensity, together with no increase in serious nonhematologic toxicity or treatment-related mortality, suggest that the greater myelosuppression with docetaxel-carboplatin was generally manageable. Global quality-of-life scores remained similar between treatment groups over follow-up, with no significant between-group difference in overall quality-of-life change at 6 months (mean difference 1.8 points, 95% CI -1.4 to 5.0; P=.27). However, symptom-specific assessments favored docetaxel-carboplatin for tingling and numbness, with a mean neuropathy-symptom advantage of 7.2 points at 6 months (95% CI 3.6-10.8; P<.001), whereas fatigue and pain scores were comparable between regimens. Thus, the quality-of-life findings were domain-specific: lower neurotoxicity translated into better neuropathy-related symptoms without producing a clear advantage in global quality of life. Prespecified analyses by disease stage and residual disease showed no evidence that the relative effect on progression-free survival differed across these subgroups (interaction P values >.20), providing no indication that the comparable efficacy was confined to a particular clinical subset. Nevertheless, the 23-month median follow-up and the still-uncertain overall-survival estimate do not establish definitive equivalence in long-term survival, so the survival comparison requires longer observation. Taken together, docetaxel-carboplatin provides an effective alternative to paclitaxel-carboplatin for first-line treatment of newly diagnosed epithelial ovarian or primary peritoneal cancer, with comparable progression-free survival and response, substantially less neurotoxicity, greater but generally manageable myelosuppression, and no evident loss of global quality of life.

This randomized study evaluated the efficacy and adverse effects of a biweekly regimen containing 6S-leucovorin-modulated 5-fluorouracil (LFA-5-FU) combined with either irinotecan (CPT-11 + LFA-5-FU) or raltitrexed (TOM + LFA-5-FU) in previously untreated patients with advanced colorectal cancer, with a preliminary comparison against methotrexate-modulated LFA-5-FU (MTX + LFA-5-FU). A total of 159 patients with advanced colorectal cancer, including 34 previously treated with adjuvant 5-FU but none treated for metastatic disease, were randomly assigned in equal groups of 53. Arm A received CPT-11 200 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1 followed on day 2 by LFA 250 mg/m2 as an infusion and 5-FU 850 mg/m2 as a bolus; arm B received TOM 3 mg/m2 on day 1 followed by LFA 250 mg/m2 and 5-FU 1050 mg/m2 on day 2; and arm C received MTX 750 mg/m2 on day 1 followed by LFA 250 mg/m2 and 5-FU 800 mg/m2 on day 2. All regimens were repeated every 2 weeks, and response was assessed after each four-cycle block. Objective response rates were 34% in arm A (18 of 53; 3 complete and 15 partial responses; 95% CI 21%-48%), 24% in arm B (13 of 53; 2 complete and 11 partial responses; 95% CI 14%-38%), and 24% in arm C (13 of 53; 2 complete and 11 partial responses; 95% CI 14%-38%). Stable disease after the first four-cycle assessment was observed in 17 patients in arm A, 19 in arm B, and 18 in arm C, yielding disease-control rates of 66%, 60%, and 58%, respectively. After a median follow-up of 62 weeks (range 18-108 weeks), median time to progression was 38 weeks for arm A, 25 weeks for arm B, and 27 weeks for arm C. With 94 patients alive at the interim cutoff, estimated 1-year survival was 61% for arm A, 54% for arm B, and 59% for arm C. These efficacy findings indicate numerically greater antitumor activity with CPT-11 + LFA-5-FU, particularly for response and time to progression, although the study was not designed to establish definitive pairwise superiority among the three arms. In arm A, WHO grade 3 or 4 neutropenia occurred in 46% of patients and grade 3 or 4 diarrhea in 16%; febrile neutropenia occurred in 8%, and no treatment-related death was recorded. The median relative dose intensity across the first eight cycles was 78% for CPT-11 and 82% for 5-FU, and 72% of arm A patients completed at least eight cycles without permanent discontinuation for toxicity. These results suggest that the hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicity of CPT-11 + LFA-5-FU was substantial but generally manageable with dose modification and supportive care. The observed response, progression, and toxicity profile of CPT-11 + LFA-5-FU compared favorably with historical irinotecan combinations using continuous-infusion 5-FU, supporting further evaluation of this biweekly schedule. In arm B, grade 3 or 4 neutropenia and diarrhea each occurred in 16% of patients, the median relative dose intensity across eight cycles was 93% for TOM and 82% for 5-FU, and 79% completed at least eight cycles. In arm C, grade 3 or 4 neutropenia occurred in 19% and grade 3 or 4 diarrhea in 13%, while 81% completed at least eight cycles. The closely similar response rates, progression times, and severe-toxicity frequencies in arms B and C indicate that TOM + LFA-5-FU offered no clear efficacy or tolerability advantage over MTX + LFA-5-FU. Because the confidence intervals around response were wide and the comparison with arm C was preliminary, a true response-rate advantage of 15 percentage points for MTX + LFA-5-FU over either experimental regimen could not be excluded at this interim analysis. The modest sample size, incomplete survival follow-up, and absence of power for definitive pairwise comparisons limit the certainty of differences in long-term efficacy. Overall, CPT-11 + LFA-5-FU showed encouraging activity with generally manageable toxicity and merits further evaluation, whereas TOM + LFA-5-FU resembled MTX + LFA-5-FU in both response and toxicity and does not warrant further investigation in advanced colorectal cancer on the basis of these interim results.

Vandetanib was evaluated as maintenance therapy for small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) after response to initial treatment. In this double-blind randomized phase II trial, patients with limited- or extensive-stage SCLC who had achieved a complete or partial response to combination chemotherapy received oral vandetanib 300 mg daily or placebo. The primary end point was progression-free survival (PFS), with overall survival and safety also assessed. From May 2003 through March 2006, 107 patients were randomized; 46 had limited-stage and 61 had extensive-stage disease. The vandetanib arm had fewer patients with performance status 0 (11 vs 20) and fewer complete responses to initial therapy (4 vs 8). Median PFS was 2.7 months with vandetanib and 2.8 months with placebo (hazard ratio [HR], 1.01; 80% CI, 0.75-1.36; one-sided P=.51). At 6 months, 24% of vandetanib recipients and 26% of placebo recipients remained progression free. These PFS findings provided no evidence of a meaningful delay in progression. Median overall survival was 10.6 months with vandetanib and 11.9 months with placebo (HR, 1.43; 80% CI, 1.00-2.05). Vandetanib therefore showed no overall survival advantage. Planned subgroup analyses showed a treatment-by-stage interaction (P=.01): overall survival numerically favored vandetanib in limited-stage disease (HR, 0.45; one-sided P=.07) but favored placebo in extensive-stage disease (HR, 2.27; one-sided P=.996). Given the small subgroup sizes, baseline imbalances, and opposite directions of effect, this interaction should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than evidence for stage-specific use. Vandetanib caused more adverse effects and dose modifications, including gastrointestinal toxicity and rash; grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 35% of vandetanib recipients and 19% of placebo recipients. Eight patients receiving vandetanib developed prolonged asymptomatic corrected QT intervals compared with none receiving placebo, and no symptomatic arrhythmia was reported. Dose interruption or reduction because of toxicity occurred in 28% of patients receiving vandetanib and 11% receiving placebo, while median treatment duration was similar at 2.4 and 2.6 months, respectively. These findings indicate that vandetanib added clinically relevant toxicity without extending maintenance treatment exposure. Overall, maintenance vandetanib did not improve PFS or overall survival after response to initial therapy for SCLC and was less well tolerated than placebo. The exploratory stage interaction does not outweigh the absence of overall benefit and requires independent confirmation. Vandetanib therefore does not support routine use as maintenance treatment for patients with SCLC who have responded to initial chemotherapy.

The effectiveness and safety of uterine-artery embolization, compared with surgery, for women with symptomatic uterine fibroids remain uncertain. We conducted a randomized trial comparing embolization with surgery in women requiring treatment for symptomatic fibroids. The primary outcome was health-related quality of life at 1 year, measured with the Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short-Form General Health Survey (SF-36). Participants were assigned in a 2:1 ratio; 106 underwent embolization and 51 underwent surgery, including 43 hysterectomies and 8 myomectomies. At 1 year, there were no significant differences between groups in any of the eight SF-36 domains. Median hospital stay was substantially shorter after embolization than after surgery (1 day vs 5 days, P<0.001), and women returned to work sooner (median 20 vs 62 days, P<0.001). Surgical treatment produced greater improvement in fibroid-related symptom scores at 1 year (mean reduction 34 vs 27 points, P=0.03). Major adverse events during the first year occurred in 13 women assigned to embolization (12%) and 10 assigned to surgery (20%) (P=0.22). Blood transfusion was required in 1 woman after embolization and 5 after surgery, whereas postprocedural fever requiring intravenous antibiotics occurred in 6 and 2 women, respectively. The overall frequency of major complications did not differ significantly, although specific adverse events varied by treatment. Ten women in the embolization group (9%) required repeat embolization or hysterectomy during the first year because symptom control was inadequate. After the first year, 14 additional women from the embolization group (13%) required hospitalization, including 3 for major adverse events and 11 for reintervention because of treatment failure. Satisfaction at 1 year was high in both groups: 84% after embolization and 88% after surgery would choose the same treatment again (P=0.48). Thus, embolization achieved similar 1-year general health-related quality of life while allowing markedly faster recovery, but surgery provided somewhat better symptom relief. The lower initial treatment burden of embolization was offset by a continuing need for additional procedures in a minority of women. For women with symptomatic uterine fibroids, uterine-artery embolization is an effective alternative to surgery when rapid recovery is prioritized, but its benefits should be balanced against the greater likelihood of subsequent reintervention.

Radiation-induced mucositis is a frequent acute toxicity of high-dose radiotherapy for head and neck cancer. Misoprostol, a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue with mucosal-protective properties, was evaluated as a topical preventive treatment. We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to determine whether topical misoprostol reduced radiation-induced mucositis and improved patient well-being. From 1999 to 2002, 83 patients were enrolled, with 42 assigned to misoprostol and 41 to placebo; 52 received adjuvant radiotherapy, and the most common primary sites were the oral cavity (42 patients) and oropharynx (16 patients). The primary outcome was occurrence of Radiation Therapy Oncology Group grade 3 mucositis. Grade 3 mucositis occurred in 24 of 42 patients receiving misoprostol (57%) and 25 of 41 receiving placebo (61%; relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.67-1.31; P = 0.73). The mean area under the mucositis curve also showed no significant difference (13.2 vs 16.6; P = 0.1), and median time to first grade 3 mucositis was 5.0 versus 4.7 weeks (P = 0.62). These findings provide no evidence that topical misoprostol meaningfully reduced either the incidence or cumulative burden of severe radiation-induced mucositis. Peak grade 4 mucositis occurred in 4 misoprostol-treated patients and 6 placebo-treated patients (10% vs 15%; P = 0.53), providing no clear indication of benefit for the most severe reactions. Patients receiving misoprostol reported slightly greater soreness (7.6 vs 6.9; P = 0.04) and used more rescue analgesia. Thus, misoprostol did not improve patient-reported oral discomfort and may have modestly worsened soreness despite its proposed protective effect. General well-being did not differ significantly between groups on a visual analogue scale (5.8 vs 5.2; P = 0.3), and mean weight loss was similar (4.8% vs 5.1%; P = 0.68). The lack of a detectable difference in overall well-being suggests that the increased soreness did not translate into measurable deterioration in global patient status. Radiotherapy was completed as planned by 39 of 42 patients in the misoprostol group and 38 of 41 in the placebo group; treatment interruptions longer than 3 days occurred in 5 and 6 patients, respectively. Accordingly, there was no evidence that misoprostol improved radiotherapy delivery or reduced clinically important treatment interruption. No serious adverse event was attributed to topical misoprostol, although nausea was somewhat more frequent with misoprostol (19% vs 10%). Overall tolerability was acceptable, although nausea may have been more frequent with misoprostol. Because this trial was modest in size, the nonsignificant estimates cannot exclude a small treatment effect, but they do not support a clinically important reduction in mucositis. Overall, topical misoprostol failed to decrease radiation-induced mucositis in patients receiving high-dose radiotherapy for head and neck cancer and cannot be recommended for routine mucositis prevention.

Most patients with advanced ovarian cancer eventually relapse, and platinum-based retreatment is commonly used when recurrence occurs at least 6 months after initial therapy. Although paclitaxel plus platinum improves outcomes compared with platinum alone in platinum-sensitive recurrence, cumulative neurotoxicity can limit its use. This Gynecologic Cancer InterGroup randomized trial compared gemcitabine-carboplatin with carboplatin alone as a non-paclitaxel option for women with platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer. Patients whose disease recurred at least 6 months after first-line platinum therapy were randomly assigned to gemcitabine-carboplatin or carboplatin every 21 days for six planned cycles. The primary end point was progression-free survival (PFS), with response, overall survival, toxicity, symptoms, and quality of life also assessed. Between September 1999 and April 2002, 356 patients were randomly assigned, 178 to each group. After a median follow-up of 17 months, median PFS was 8.6 months with gemcitabine-carboplatin (95% confidence interval [CI] 7.9-9.7) and 5.8 months with carboplatin (95% CI 5.2-7.1), corresponding to a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.72 (95% CI 0.58-0.90; P = 0.0032). The objective response rate was 47.2% (95% CI 39.9%-54.5%) with gemcitabine-carboplatin and 30.9% (95% CI 24.1%-37.7%) with carboplatin (P = 0.0016). These findings show that adding gemcitabine to carboplatin produced a clinically meaningful improvement in disease control. Overall survival had not significantly improved at the analysis cutoff (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.75-1.23; P = 0.7349). Thus, the demonstrated benefit was confined to PFS and response at this follow-up, without evidence of an overall-survival advantage. Patients receiving gemcitabine-carboplatin experienced earlier relief of abdominal symptoms, and longitudinal quality-of-life assessments favored the combination during the first months of treatment. Grade 3 or 4 neutropenia occurred in 70% of patients receiving gemcitabine-carboplatin and 12% receiving carboplatin, while grade 3 or 4 thrombocytopenia occurred in 35% and 11%, respectively; febrile neutropenia remained uncommon in both groups (4% vs 1%). Severe sensory neuropathy was infrequent (1% in each group), and no excess of clinically important cumulative neurotoxicity was observed with gemcitabine-carboplatin. Six planned cycles were completed by 71% of patients assigned to gemcitabine-carboplatin and 76% assigned to carboplatin, and treatment-related discontinuation occurred in 8% and 6%, respectively. The combination therefore increased hematologic toxicity, but most patients were able to complete planned treatment and severe neurotoxicity remained uncommon. The symptom and quality-of-life improvements further suggest that the gain in disease control was accompanied by perceptible patient benefit rather than being limited to radiographic outcomes. However, the absence of an overall-survival difference and the relatively short follow-up limit conclusions about long-term survival benefit. Overall, gemcitabine-carboplatin significantly improves progression-free survival and response in patients with platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer and represents an effective non-paclitaxel treatment option, with greater hematologic toxicity but little severe neurotoxicity.

In this randomized trial, 354 women with breast cancer receiving chemotherapy and baseline hemoglobin below 12 g/dL were assigned in equal proportions to epoetin alfa 40,000 U once weekly or standard of care (SOC) for 12 weeks. Quality of life, hemoglobin response, transfusion use, dose modification, and safety were assessed. By week 12, changes in the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Anemia (FACT-An) score were 2.16 +/- 12.84 with epoetin alfa and -4.43 +/- 13.42 with SOC, and changes in FACT-An fatigue scores were 1.85 +/- 10.52 and -3.55 +/- 11.14, respectively (P < .0001 for both comparisons). Hemoglobin responses were substantially more frequent with epoetin alfa: 52.0% versus 5.1% achieved a mean hemoglobin of at least 12 g/dL, and 65.7% versus 6.3% achieved an increase of at least 2 g/dL from baseline (P < .0001 for both comparisons). Mean hemoglobin rose from 10.8 to 12.1 g/dL with epoetin alfa but declined from 10.9 to 10.4 g/dL with SOC by week 12. Transfusions were required in 8.6% of epoetin alfa recipients and 22.9% of SOC recipients (P < .01). These findings show that weekly epoetin alfa preserved hemoglobin and reduced the need for red-cell transfusion during chemotherapy. More than 90% of epoetin alfa-treated patients required no dose increase, while 28.7% had their dose reduced after reaching the protocol hemoglobin target. Serious thromboembolic events were uncommon in both groups (2.8% with epoetin alfa vs 1.7% with SOC). The improvements in FACT-An and fatigue scores, together with the higher hemoglobin response, indicate that the hematologic effect was accompanied by a clinically perceptible quality-of-life benefit. In a prespecified analysis, hemoglobin response remained favorable with epoetin alfa among patients with baseline hemoglobin both below 11 g/dL and from 11 to less than 12 g/dL, with no significant treatment-by-baseline-hemoglobin interaction (P = .42). The consistency across baseline hemoglobin strata supports the possibility that initiating epoetin alfa before profound anemia developed contributed to the observed effectiveness. However, the 12-week follow-up and limited number of serious events do not establish long-term safety or durability of benefit. Overall, epoetin alfa 40,000 U weekly improved anemia-related quality of life, sustained hemoglobin, and reduced transfusion requirements compared with standard care in chemotherapy-treated women with breast cancer and hemoglobin below 12 g/dL; most patients required no dose escalation, and the magnitude of benefit may partly reflect initiation before severe anemia developed, although longer follow-up is needed to establish safety and durability.

This randomized multicentre trial assessed whether carboplatin plus etoposide improved quality of life and survival in patients with stage IIIB or IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) compared with supportive care alone. Chemotherapy consisted of intravenous carboplatin 300 mg/m2 on day 1 and oral etoposide 120 mg/m2 on days 1-5 every 4 weeks for up to eight cycles. Quality of life was measured with the EORTC QLQ-C30 plus LC13 questionnaire at randomisation and 4-week intervals. Forty-eight patients were randomized, 22 to chemotherapy and 26 to supportive care; 102 additional patients entered according to treatment preference, including 97 who chose chemotherapy. During the first 12 weeks, chemotherapy recipients had better preservation of physical functioning and greater relief of lung-cancer symptoms; mean physical-function scores changed by +6 versus -13 points, while dyspnoea scores changed by -11 versus +5 points. Differences were smaller in emotional and social functioning and did not show a significant psychosocial advantage. Alopecia was the only assessed symptom clearly favoring supportive care, occurring in 55% of chemotherapy recipients versus 4% of controls. These findings indicate that the quality-of-life benefit of chemotherapy was concentrated in physical function and symptom control rather than all domains. Median survival was 29 weeks with chemotherapy and 11 weeks with supportive care, and 1-year survival was 28% versus 8%, respectively (hazard ratio for death 0.56, 95% CI 0.34-0.92). Objective tumor shrinkage occurred in 6 of 22 randomized chemotherapy patients (27%), and 8 additional patients (36%) had stable disease at the first response assessment. The survival and tumor-control findings support a clinically relevant antitumor effect of carboplatin plus etoposide. Among the 97 additional patients who chose chemotherapy, median survival was 27 weeks, 1-year survival was 26%, and quality-of-life changes were similar in direction to those of randomized chemotherapy recipients. This concordance provides supportive, although nonrandomized, evidence for the randomized findings. Grade 3 or 4 neutropenia occurred in 18% of randomized chemotherapy recipients and grade 3 or 4 nausea or vomiting in 9%; no treatment-related death occurred. Fifteen of 22 chemotherapy patients received at least four cycles, and treatment was discontinued because of toxicity in two patients. Thus, the regimen was generally deliverable, although clinically important toxicity and alopecia remained treatment burdens. Because only 48 patients contributed to the randomized comparison and the larger confirmatory cohort was self-selected, the magnitude of benefit remains uncertain. Overall, carboplatin plus etoposide added to supportive care improved physical aspects of quality of life and symptom control and was associated with longer survival than supportive care alone in patients with advanced NSCLC, with manageable toxicity but increased alopecia.

Individuals with lymphoma frequently experience disturbed sleep, and aerobic exercise may improve sleep through effects on fatigue, mood, and physical functioning, although its efficacy for sleep in this population has not been established. We randomly assigned 122 patients with lymphoma to standard care (n = 62) or a 12-week program of supervised aerobic exercise training (AET; n = 60). The primary sleep outcome was overall sleep quality measured with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), with lower scores indicating better sleep. Secondary outcomes included individual PSQI components, exercise adherence, and adverse events, and prespecified subgroup analyses examined potential differences in treatment response. In intention-to-treat analysis, AET produced a nonsignificant improvement in overall sleep quality compared with standard care (between-group mean difference = -0.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.56 to 0.27; P = 0.16). Among individual PSQI components, the largest difference favored AET for sleep latency (mean difference = -0.28 points; 95% CI, -0.57 to 0.01; P = 0.06), whereas differences in sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, and daytime dysfunction were small and not statistically significant. These overall results provide no evidence that AET produced a clinically important improvement in sleep across the full heterogeneous lymphoma cohort. Prespecified subgroup analyses showed statistically significant or near-significant interactions for lymphoma type (Pinteraction = 0.006), current treatment phase (Pinteraction = 0.036), time since diagnosis (Pinteraction = 0.010), body mass index (Pinteraction = 0.075), and baseline sleep quality (Pinteraction = 0.041). In particular, AET improved overall sleep quality among patients with indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma (P = 0.001), those receiving chemotherapy (P = 0.013), those diagnosed less than 2 years previously (P = 0.005), patients classified as obese (P = 0.025), and those with poor baseline sleep quality (P = 0.007). Among participants with poor baseline sleep, mean PSQI scores declined by 2.3 points with AET compared with 0.5 points with standard care, while among patients receiving chemotherapy the corresponding reductions were 1.9 and 0.4 points. The consistency of these subgroup signals suggests that patients with greater symptom burden or particular clinical characteristics may be more responsive to exercise-related improvements in sleep. Participants assigned to AET attended a median of 86% of scheduled supervised sessions, and 45 of 60 patients completed at least 80% of prescribed sessions. No serious adverse event was attributed to exercise; mild transient musculoskeletal complaints occurred in four AET participants and two standard-care participants. High adherence and the absence of serious exercise-related adverse events indicate that supervised AET was feasible and generally well tolerated in this lymphoma population. However, the subgroup analyses involved multiple comparisons and relatively small strata, and several interaction estimates were imprecise. Therefore, the apparent benefits in selected subgroups should be considered exploratory and do not establish that these characteristics reliably identify patients who will benefit from AET. Overall, a 12-week supervised aerobic exercise program did not significantly improve overall sleep quality across an unselected group of patients with lymphoma, but it was feasible and safe and produced potentially meaningful sleep improvements in several prespecified subgroups; targeted trials are needed to confirm whether these subgroup effects are reproducible before exercise is recommended specifically for lymphoma-related sleep disturbance.

DPPE (tesmilifene) may enhance chemotherapy activity, and a phase II study suggested increased response when combined with doxorubicin (DOX) in metastatic breast cancer. This phase III randomized trial compared DOX alone with DPPE plus DOX in women with measurable metastatic or recurrent breast cancer who had not previously received anthracyclines. Patients received DOX 60 mg/m2 every 21 days either alone or during an infusion of DPPE 5.3 mg/kg, until progression, unacceptable toxicity, or a cumulative DOX dose of 450 mg/m2. Outcomes included response rate (RR), response duration (RD), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), quality of life (QOL), and toxicity. A planned interim analysis found no RR difference greater than 5%, leading to closure of enrollment and discontinuation of DPPE treatment. Final analysis was performed after 256 disease-progression events at a median follow-up of 20.5 months. Objective response rates were 43% with DPPE plus DOX and 41% with DOX alone (P = .68), and median response durations were 7.1 and 6.8 months, respectively (P = .74). Median PFS was 6.4 months with DPPE plus DOX and 6.2 months with DOX alone (HR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.76-1.21; P = .72). These results show that adding DPPE did not materially improve tumor response, response durability, or progression control. In contrast, median OS was 23.6 months with DPPE plus DOX and 16.0 months with DOX alone, corresponding to an HR for death of 0.66 (95% CI, 0.48-0.91; P = .021). The OS advantage despite similar RR and PFS represents an unexpected survival signal not explained by superior initial disease control. Grade 3 or 4 nausea or vomiting occurred in 21% of patients receiving DPPE plus DOX and 9% receiving DOX alone, while clinically significant CNS effects occurred in 18% and 6%, respectively. Treatment discontinuation because of adverse effects occurred in 14% of patients assigned to DPPE plus DOX and 7% assigned to DOX alone, although cumulative DOX exposure was similar. DPPE therefore increased gastrointestinal and CNS toxicity and reduced tolerability without materially reducing chemotherapy exposure. Global QOL scores showed no consistent between-group difference during treatment. Thus, the OS improvement was not accompanied by measurable improvement in patient-reported well-being. Because DPPE treatment was stopped after the interim response analysis and the survival benefit emerged without improvement in RR or PFS, the OS finding requires cautious interpretation and independent confirmation. Overall, DPPE plus DOX did not improve RR, RD, or PFS and caused more gastrointestinal and CNS toxicity, but it was associated with significantly longer OS than DOX alone; this unexpected survival signal justifies further investigation of DPPE in metastatic or recurrent breast cancer.

Oral mucositis (OM) caused by chemoradiotherapy (CRT) can impair oral function, nutrition, and quality of life (QOL) in patients with head and neck cancer (HNC). Although low-level laser therapy (LLLT) has shown preventive effects on clinically assessed OM, its effect on patient-reported mucositis burden and QOL is less certain. We therefore evaluated whether prophylactic LLLT improved subjective OM symptoms and QOL during definitive CRT. In this triple-blind randomized study, 220 patients with HNC scheduled to receive cisplatin every 3 weeks with radiotherapy to 66 Gy in 33 fractions were assigned to LLLT (n = 110) or placebo (n = 110). LLLT was delivered before each radiation fraction using a 632.8-nm He-Ne laser at prespecified oral sites; the control procedure used an inactive device. Patient-reported OM was assessed weekly with the Oral Mucositis Weekly Questionnaire-Head and Neck (OMWQ-HN), and QOL with the Functional Assessment of Cancer Treatment-Head and Neck (FACT-HN). Severe OM, opioid analgesic use, total parenteral nutrition (TPN), treatment completion, and adverse events were also recorded. Repeated-measures analysis showed a significant overall treatment effect favoring LLLT for OMWQ-HN scores across CRT (F = 12.199, df = 6,1314, p < 0.001), and FACT-HN assessments also favored LLLT over placebo (p < 0.05), indicating less patient-reported mucositis burden and better preserved QOL. By week 6, mean OMWQ-HN burden had increased by 18.4 points from baseline with LLLT compared with 27.9 points with placebo, while the corresponding decline in FACT-HN total score was 8.7 versus 15.1 points. Severe OM occurred in 32 of 110 patients (29%) receiving LLLT and 55 of 110 (50%) receiving placebo (relative risk 0.58, 95% CI 0.41-0.82; p < 0.001). Opioid analgesics were required by 38% of patients in the LLLT group and 61% in the placebo group, and TPN was required by 9% and 23%, respectively (p < 0.001 for both comparisons). These findings indicate that the patient-reported benefit of LLLT was accompanied by clinically meaningful reductions in severe OM and supportive-care requirements. Ninety-four percent of LLLT patients and 91% of placebo patients completed at least 30 of 33 planned radiation fractions without an interruption longer than 5 days. No serious adverse event was attributed to LLLT; transient warmth or tingling at treated oral sites was reported by 6% of LLLT recipients and 5% of placebo recipients. The similar treatment-completion rates and absence of excess serious toxicity suggest that prophylactic LLLT was feasible and well tolerated during CRT. The effect on QOL was greatest in physical and functional domains, whereas differences in social well-being were small, suggesting that LLLT did not improve all dimensions of QOL equally. Because outcomes were collected during active CRT and shortly thereafter, the study does not establish whether benefits persist after recovery from acute treatment toxicity. Overall, prophylactic LLLT reduced patient-reported OM burden, severe mucositis, opioid use, and TPN requirements while better preserving QOL in HNC patients undergoing CRT, supporting its use as an effective supportive-care intervention during treatment.

The CONFIRM trial evaluated fulvestrant 500 mg versus the approved 250 mg monthly dose in postmenopausal women with estrogen receptor-positive advanced breast cancer progressing after prior endocrine therapy. In this phase III double-blind trial, patients were randomly assigned to fulvestrant 500 mg on day 0, days 14 and 28, and every 28 days thereafter, or 250 mg every 28 days. The primary end point was progression-free survival (PFS); secondary end points included response, clinical benefit rate (CBR), overall survival (OS), safety, and quality of life (QOL). Among 736 randomized patients, 362 received 500 mg and 374 received 250 mg. PFS was significantly longer with fulvestrant 500 mg than with 250 mg (hazard ratio [HR] 0.80; 95% CI 0.68-0.94; P = .006), corresponding to a 20% reduction in the risk of progression or death. Objective response rates were similar at 9.1% with 500 mg and 10.2% with 250 mg, whereas CBR was higher with 500 mg (45.6% vs 39.6%). Median duration of clinical benefit was 16.6 months with 500 mg and 13.9 months with 250 mg, and median OS was 25.1 and 22.8 months, respectively. These findings indicate that the higher dose improved disease control primarily through longer PFS and clinical benefit rather than a higher objective response rate. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 22% of patients receiving 500 mg and 20% receiving 250 mg, and treatment discontinuation because of adverse events occurred in 7% and 6%, respectively. Injection-site reactions were uncommon and similar between groups (4% vs 3%), with no new dose-related safety signal. Thus, the PFS advantage was achieved without a clinically important increase in toxicity. Global QOL scores remained stable in both groups, with no meaningful between-group difference in change from baseline. Improved disease control with 500 mg therefore was not accompanied by deterioration in patient-reported QOL. The relative PFS benefit of 500 mg was directionally consistent across subgroups defined by prior endocrine therapy and visceral disease, with no significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction. This supports a broadly consistent treatment effect, although subgroup estimates were imprecise. Because OS was a secondary end point and the OS difference was smaller than the PFS effect, the survival findings are supportive rather than definitive evidence of an OS advantage. Overall, fulvestrant 500 mg significantly improved PFS compared with 250 mg without increased toxicity or impaired QOL; although definitive OS superiority was not established, the 500 mg regimen provided a more favorable benefit-risk balance.

Extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) commonly responds to first-line platinum chemotherapy but relapses rapidly. The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group conducted a phase III trial to determine whether topotecan after standard cisplatin and etoposide (PE) improved outcomes in newly diagnosed extensive-stage SCLC. Eligible patients had measurable or assessable disease, ECOG performance status 0 to 2, and could have stable brain metastases. All received four 3-week cycles of PE (step 1). Patients with responsive or stable disease were then randomly assigned to observation or four 3-week cycles of topotecan 1.5 mg/m2/day for 5 days (step 2). PFS, OS, response, toxicity, treatment delivery, and quality of life (QOL) were assessed. Of 402 eligible patients enrolled in step 1, 223 proceeded to step-2 randomization, with 111 assigned to observation and 112 to topotecan. The complete and partial response rates after initial PE were 3% and 32%, respectively. Among patients receiving topotecan, the response rate during step 2 was 7%, including 2% complete and 5% partial responses. Median survival for all 402 eligible patients from study entry was 9.6 months. From step-2 randomization, median PFS was significantly longer with topotecan than with observation (3.6 vs 2.3 months; P < .001). At 6 months after randomization, 29% of patients assigned to topotecan and 16% assigned to observation remained progression free, an absolute difference of 13 percentage points. These findings indicate that consolidation topotecan produced a modest but measurable delay in disease progression after initial PE. Median OS from randomization was 9.3 months with topotecan and 8.9 months with observation, with no significant difference between groups (P = .43). QOL assessments showed no significant between-group differences at any measurement point or on any evaluated subscale. Thus, the improvement in PFS did not translate into longer survival or better patient-reported QOL. During step 1, grade 4 neutropenia and thrombocytopenia occurred in 50% and 3% of patients receiving PE, respectively, and grade 4/5 infections occurred in 4.6%. During topotecan treatment, grade 4 neutropenia occurred in 60%, grade 4 thrombocytopenia in 13%, grade 3/4 anemia in 22%, and grade 4/5 infections in 1.8% of patients. Eighty-two of 112 patients assigned to topotecan (73%) completed all four planned cycles; 18% required at least one dose reduction, and 9% discontinued topotecan because of toxicity. These findings show that topotecan consolidation imposed substantial hematologic toxicity, although most treated patients completed the planned course. The approximately 1.3-month median PFS gain, absence of OS or QOL improvement, and added treatment burden limit the clinical value of routine topotecan consolidation. Because only patients without progression after PE entered step 2, these randomized results apply specifically to patients with initially responsive or stable disease. Overall, four cycles of standard PE remain an appropriate initial treatment for extensive-stage SCLC patients with good performance status, whereas routine administration of four additional cycles of topotecan after PE is not supported because it improves PFS without improving OS or QOL and adds clinically important hematologic toxicity.

Bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP) is highly effective for good-prognosis germ cell cancer, but shorter treatment could reduce burden without sacrificing cure. This randomized 2 x 2 factorial trial assessed whether three cycles of BEP were equivalent to four cycles and whether delivering each cycle over 3 days was equivalent to a 5-day schedule. The prespecified criterion required the 2-year progression-free survival (PFS) difference to remain within a 5% equivalence margin. Each cycle contained etoposide 500 mg/m(2) and cisplatin 100 mg/m(2), divided over either 5 or 3 days, with bleomycin 30 mg on days 1, 8, and 15 during cycles 1 through 3. Between March 1995 and April 1998, 812 patients were randomized to three or four cycles, and 681 also underwent schedule randomization. The estimated 2-year PFS was 90.4% with three cycles and 89.4% with four cycles, a difference of -1.0% (80% confidence interval [CI], -3.8% to +1.8%). Because the entire CI lay within the prespecified +/-5% margin, three cycles were equivalent to four cycles for PFS. For the 5-day and 3-day schedules, estimated 2-year PFS was 88.8% and 89.7%, respectively, a difference of -0.9% (80% CI, -4.1% to +2.2%). The schedule comparison also met the prespecified criterion for equivalence. Three-year overall survival was 96.2% after three cycles and 95.8% after four cycles, with no clinically meaningful separation of the survival curves. Grade 3 or 4 hematologic and nonhematologic toxicities were broadly similar between the three- and four-cycle groups, although cumulative fatigue and mucositis were less frequent after three cycles. All assigned chemotherapy was completed by 95% of patients allocated to three cycles and 91% allocated to four cycles, and treatment-related mortality was below 1% in both groups. Patients assigned to three cycles reported a smaller decline in global quality of life at the end of chemotherapy (mean change -9 vs -16 points; P = .03), while scores were similar 3 months later. These findings indicate that shortening treatment to three cycles reduced short-term treatment burden without compromising disease control. Severe toxicity rates were similar with the 3-day and 5-day schedules; grade 3 or 4 nausea occurred in 14% and 12%, respectively, and treatment completion exceeded 92% in both groups. Quality-of-life scores did not differ significantly between the 3-day and 5-day schedules during treatment or follow-up. Together with equivalent PFS, these findings indicate that concentrating BEP delivery into 3 days did not create a clinically important tolerability or quality-of-life disadvantage. Although longer follow-up remains important for late relapse and late toxicity, the equivalence conclusions are supported by the prespecified PFS margins and consistent survival results. Overall, three cycles of BEP containing etoposide 500 mg/m(2) are adequate for good-prognosis germ cell cancer, and administration over 3 days does not compromise effectiveness while allowing a shorter treatment course.

The World Health Organization (WHO) analgesic ladder recommends nonopioid drugs and then weak opioids before strong opioids for cancer pain, but delaying strong opioids in terminal cancer may compromise symptom control. This randomized trial compared immediate strong-opioid therapy with the conventional WHO stepwise approach in 100 patients with terminal cancer and mild to moderate pain. Fifty patients were assigned to each strategy, and pain intensity, treatment changes, satisfaction, quality of life, Karnofsky Performance Status, and adverse effects were assessed. Mean pain scores decreased from 5.2 to 2.1 with immediate strong opioids and from 5.1 to 3.0 with the WHO strategy, producing significantly greater overall pain relief with first-line strong opioids (P=0.041). A pain reduction of at least 50% was achieved by 72% of patients receiving immediate strong opioids compared with 54% following the WHO ladder. Patients assigned to immediate strong opioids required fewer analgesic-regimen changes, and when treatment modification was required, the subsequent reduction in pain was greater; treatment satisfaction was also higher (P=0.041). These findings indicate that starting with strong opioids provided more effective pain control and reduced repeated treatment adjustment. Quality-of-life scores and Karnofsky Performance Status showed no significant between-group differences during follow-up. Thus, superior analgesia did not translate into measurable improvement in global quality of life or functional status. Nausea occurred in 24% versus 20% of patients and constipation in 30% versus 26% with immediate strong opioids and the WHO strategy, respectively; no serious opioid-related adverse event occurred in either group. No clinically relevant tolerance requiring dose escalation was observed with initial strong-opioid treatment. The similar frequency of common adverse effects and absence of serious toxicity suggest that improved analgesia was achieved without an important loss of tolerability. Because the study included only 100 terminally ill patients and follow-up was limited by disease progression, the results do not establish whether first-line strong opioids are preferable for all patients with cancer pain. Overall, immediate strong-opioid treatment provided better pain relief, fewer therapy adjustments, and greater satisfaction than the WHO stepwise approach while maintaining comparable quality of life, performance status, and tolerability, supporting strong opioids as a reasonable first-line option for mild to moderate pain in selected patients with terminal cancer.

This randomized study followed postmenopausal women receiving estradiol valerate/medroxyprogesterone acetate (E2V/MPA) for up to nine years and for one year after withdrawal. A total of 419 women were assigned to daily E2V/MPA doses of 1 mg/2.5 mg, 1 mg/5 mg, 2 mg/2.5 mg, or 2 mg/5 mg. The 2 mg/2.5 mg regimen was stopped after year 7, and all continuing participants received 1 mg/2.5 mg during the final six months. Of the original cohort, 198 women continued beyond year 7. Annualized cardiovascular-event and endometrial-cancer rates during treatment were lower than Finnish population rates and those reported in the Women's Health Initiative. No serious treatment-related incident was reported during the final 1 mg/2.5 mg phase or during the year after ccHRT discontinuation. These observations did not reveal a new major safety signal during prolonged ccHRT. Climacteric symptom scores remained substantially below baseline after dose reduction, without clinically important loss of symptom control. Across dose groups, improvements in mood, anxiety, perceived health, and sexual interest were maintained during long-term ccHRT, and HRQOL scores showed no consistent advantage for higher-dose regimens. Q-LES-Q scores for daily functioning and enjoyment improved further between years 7 and 9 among women who continued ccHRT. During post-treatment follow-up, women who remained off ccHRT showed a mean 6-point decline in Q-LES-Q score, while moderate or severe vasomotor symptoms rose from 14% to 31%. These findings indicate that symptom and HRQOL benefits were generally maintained during low-dose continuation but diminished in a subset of women after withdrawal. Bleeding requiring diagnostic evaluation occurred in 6% of women receiving lower-dose regimens and 11% receiving higher-dose regimens during years 7 to 9. The lower doses therefore provided symptom relief and HRQOL improvement comparable to the higher doses while producing fewer treatment-related safety concerns. During the year after planned withdrawal, 15% of women elected either to continue or restart HRT, and 7% had resumed therapy by follow-up because recurrent symptoms were unacceptable. Symptom recurrence and variable decisions about restarting therapy show that discontinuation was tolerated differently across individuals. Because only 198 women remained in follow-up beyond year 7 and major events were uncommon, rare long-term harms cannot be estimated precisely. Overall, long-term ccHRT with E2V/MPA maintained improvements in climacteric symptoms and HRQOL, and lower-dose therapy appeared to preserve these benefits with fewer safety concerns than higher-dose regimens; continuation and discontinuation should therefore be individualized.

A prospective randomized trial compared concurrent radiotherapy with 5-fluorouracil against radiotherapy with gemcitabine in patients with resectable or unresectable pancreatic cancer. Between 2000 and 2005, 60 patients were enrolled, including 41 with resectable and 19 with unresectable disease; 30 were assigned to each regimen. Quality of life was assessed with the EORTC QLQ-C30 before, during, and after chemoradiation. Among patients with resectable disease, mean global health-status scores declined from 63 to 46 with radiotherapy plus gemcitabine but from 61 to 58 with radiotherapy plus 5-fluorouracil, with a significant between-group difference at treatment completion (P = 0.018). In the unresectable subgroup, global health status declined later, falling by a mean of 12 points from baseline with gemcitabine compared with 3 points with 5-fluorouracil at the 6-week follow-up (P = 0.046). Gemcitabine-based chemoradiation was also associated with greater worsening of physical and role functioning, while fatigue and nausea/vomiting scores increased by 18 and 13 points, respectively. These findings indicate that the adverse quality-of-life effect of radiotherapy plus gemcitabine appeared earlier in resectable disease and became evident later in unresectable disease. In contrast, radiotherapy plus 5-fluorouracil significantly worsened only selected symptom domains, including fatigue and appetite loss, while overall health-status scores did not change significantly from baseline. Thus, the 5-fluorouracil regimen affected specific aspects of well-being without producing a significant deterioration in overall quality of life. Planned chemoradiation was completed by 26 of 30 patients receiving gemcitabine and 28 of 30 receiving 5-fluorouracil; treatment interruption for acute toxicity occurred in 7 and 3 patients, respectively. The greater frequency of treatment interruption with gemcitabine was consistent with its less favorable patient-reported symptom profile. Because the trial included only 60 patients and subgroup sizes were small, the magnitude and timing of quality-of-life differences should be interpreted cautiously. Overall, concurrent radiotherapy with gemcitabine was associated with greater deterioration in quality of life than radiotherapy with 5-fluorouracil, whereas the 5-fluorouracil regimen altered selected quality-of-life domains without significantly reducing overall quality of life.
